prompt: A landscape shows dusty red rocks and an ancient-looking channel. Which conclusion is best supported?
option_B: It could be Mars, but colour alone is insufficient
option_C: It must be a desert on Earth
option_D: The channel proves running water exists today
clue_1: Iron-rich minerals can appear reddish on more than one planet.
clue_2: Other observations, including atmosphere and geology, would help identify the world.
explanation: The colour of rocks is an observation. Identifying a planet from colour alone is an inference that needs more evidence.
misconception: A red surface proves the location is Mars.

round: A2 · Colours That Are Not There
prompt: An astronomical image uses brilliant purple and green regions. What must be checked before interpreting the colours?
option_A: Whether assigned colours represent different wavelengths
option_B: Whether the image was taken at night
option_C: Whether the telescope is on Earth
option_D: Whether the stars have stopped moving
clue_1: Telescopes can detect light outside the wavelengths visible to humans.
clue_2: Scientists sometimes assign visible colours to wavelengths or measurements.
explanation: False-colour or representative-colour processing can convey scientific data. A colour in a published image may not be what human eyes would see.
observable_evidence: Different coloured patches and brightness patterns.
misconception: All astronomical image colours represent what a human eye would see.

prompt: A circular depression is seen on a rocky surface. What is the strongest scientific next step?
option_A: Assume it is a volcanic crater
option_B: Assume it is an impact crater
option_C: Compare rim, ejecta and surrounding geology
option_D: Decide from its circular shape alone
clue_1: Different processes can form circular depressions.
clue_2: Impact features may have ejecta patterns; volcanic features have other geological clues.
explanation: Shape alone is insufficient; examine surrounding evidence and consider multiple explanations.
observable_evidence: Round depression; raised edge; surrounding terrain.
misconception: Every circular crater was formed by an asteroid.

prompt: An observer records Venus appearing as a thin crescent and later nearly full. Which model explains its complete sequence of phases?
option_A: A simple Earth-centred model with Venus always between Earth and the Sun
option_B: A Sun-centred model in which Venus orbits the Sun
option_C: A model in which Venus makes its own light
clue_1: The lit fraction depends on the positions of Venus, Earth and the Sun.
clue_2: Venus can appear gibbous when it is on the far side of its orbit relative to Earth
explanation: so we see most of its sunlit hemisphere.
observable_evidence: The full sequence of Venus phases supports Venus orbiting the Sun; simple traditional Ptolemaic geometry cannot produce all the observed phases.
source_url: Galileo alone proved every detail of the modern Solar System.

prompt: Four small points change positions around Jupiter over several nights. What is the best inference?
option_B: They may be objects orbiting Jupiter
option_C: Jupiter orbits Earth once a day
clue_1: Their positions change relative to Jupiter.
clue_2: Their repeated motion is consistent with bodies orbiting Jupiter.
explanation: Galileo observed four moons orbiting Jupiter. The finding demonstrated that not every celestial body orbits Earth.
observable_evidence: Points repeatedly change sides of Jupiter.
misconception: This observation alone proves Earth orbits the Sun.

prompt: Mars appears to move backwards against background stars for a period. What explains this apparent retrograde motion?
option_B: Earth overtakes Mars in their different solar orbits
option_C: The stars physically rotate around Mars
clue_1: It is an apparent change in position relative to distant stars.
clue_2: Earth and Mars orbit the Sun at different speeds.
explanation: When faster-moving Earth overtakes Mars, the line of sight shifts so Mars appears temporarily to move backwards relative to distant stars.
observable_evidence: Direction of apparent position change over time.
misconception: Retrograde motion means a planet reverses its orbital direction.

round: C1 · Half a World in Darkness
prompt: A model shows one side of Earth illuminated and the other dark. What causes the daily cycle of daylight and darkness at a location?
option_B: The Moon passing around Earth every day
option_D: The Sun switching off at night
clue_1: Only the hemisphere facing the Sun receives direct sunlight.
clue_2: A place moves between illuminated and dark halves as Earth rotates.
explanation: Earth rotates approximately once every 24 hours relative to the Sun, producing day and night.
observable_evidence: One illuminated hemisphere and one dark hemisphere.
misconception: The Moon causes night by blocking the Sun daily.

prompt: About half the visible lunar disc is illuminated. What is justified from this image alone?
option_C: It is a quarter phase, but orientation is needed to distinguish first from third
option_D: Earth’s shadow covers half the Moon
clue_1: The Moon reflects sunlight rather than producing its own visible light.
clue_2: We see varying fractions of its sunlit hemisphere as it orbits Earth.
explanation: At a quarter phase, approximately half the disc is lit. Lit fraction alone does not establish first versus third quarter; lunar phases are not usually due to Earth’s shadow.
observable_evidence: Approximately half the lunar disc appears bright.
misconception: A half Moon is a lunar eclipse.

prompt: During a brief event, the Moon appears to cover the Sun for some observers. Which alignment is required?
clue_1: This event occurs during a new-Moon configuration.
clue_2: The Moon casts a shadow on part of Earth.
explanation: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun and its shadow reaches Earth. The Moon’s orbit is tilted, so not every new Moon produces an eclipse.
observable_evidence: Apparent overlap of two circular discs.
misconception: Every new Moon produces a solar eclipse.

prompt: A dark shape is visible against the bright Milky Way. Which explanation is scientifically appropriate?
option_A: It is a hole with no stars anywhere behind it
option_B: Dark interstellar dust obscures background starlight
option_C: It is caused by a cloud in Earth’s atmosphere
option_D: The Milky Way only has bright stars
clue_1: Look at the contrast between bright star fields and dark lanes.
clue_2: Dust within the Milky Way absorbs and scatters visible light.
explanation: The dark lanes are clouds of interstellar dust. Some Aboriginal astronomical knowledge traditions recognise a figure in this pattern; use specifically attributed, community-authorised sources when teaching cultural interpretations.
observable_evidence: Dark lanes against bright Milky Way star fields.
misconception: The cultural knowledge is interchangeable across Aboriginal Nations.

prompt: A constellation rises at different evening times through the year. What is the best explanation?
option_A: Earth’s orbital motion changes the night-time view of stars through the year
option_B: The constellation circles Earth once a year
clue_1: Record observations at the same clock time across several months.
clue_2: Earth changes position in its orbit around the Sun.
explanation: Earth’s annual revolution causes the Sun’s apparent background position to shift, changing which constellations are visible at a given evening time. Cultural seasonal calendars are place- and community-specific and must be attributed.
observable_evidence: A constellation is visible in some months and not at the same time in others.
misconception: The same seasonal interpretation applies everywhere in Australia.

prompt: ASKAP detects astronomical radio signals. What can it observe that an ordinary optical camera cannot directly detect?
clue_1: Not all electromagnetic waves are visible light.
clue_2: Radio dishes receive radio-frequency electromagnetic radiation.
explanation: ASKAP is a radio interferometer array in Western Australia; it reveals radio emission inaccessible to an ordinary visible-light camera.
observable_evidence: An array of dish antennas and signal data.
misconception: Radio telescopes listen to sound travelling through space.

prompt: Scientists want to record changing positions of Jupiter’s moons over successive nights. Which tool is most suitable?
option_B: An optical telescope and dated observation record
clue_1: The target is distant and must be magnified.
clue_2: Successive dated observations allow a movement pattern to be identified.
explanation: An optical telescope collects and resolves light, while accurate time-stamped records allow comparison across observations.
observable_evidence: Distant small points changing relative positions.
misconception: A telescope alone provides an explanation without records.

prompt: Two images of the same galaxy look different: one uses visible light, one radio observations. Which conclusion is best?
option_B: Different wavelengths reveal different physical processes
option_C: Radio imagery is an ordinary colour photograph
option_D: The galaxy has changed shape between every image
clue_2: Some sources of radio emission are not prominent in visible light.
explanation: Multiwavelength observations reveal different emissions and structures; data processing and image alignment must be considered before drawing conclusions.
observable_evidence: Different bright regions in two representations.
misconception: Only one wavelength can provide trustworthy scientific evidence.

prompt: A simulated radio source records 4, 6, 5, 11, 12 and 10 arbitrary units in six equal time intervals. Which conclusion is warranted?
option_A: The source is definitely an alien signal
option_B: Recorded values are higher in the last three intervals
option_C: The source is exactly twice as bright forever
option_D: The instrument cannot be used to compare readings
clue_1: Compare the first three readings with the final three.
clue_2: Mean values are 5 units and 11 units respectively.
explanation: The later mean is higher in this simulated dataset; we cannot infer the physical cause or long-term behaviour from six values alone. This is a teaching dataset, not real ASKAP measurements.
observable_evidence: Six ordered readings and a change in average.
misconception: A pattern proves a specific cause.
